skill-partial-scaffoldskill-scaffolding0 of 0.375 (major)failThe requirement says that when some but not all anchors are present, the skill scaffolds the missing anchors. In one delivered case the helper does not. In tests/unit/setup.test.ts &#39;rejects stubs that do not implement the contract&#39; (lines 60-69), the build anchor is present. Stub files exist under src/presentation-kit/ and src/presentations/index.ts, and detectAnchors reports kit:false and index:false, so the scenario&#39;s condition holds. The test then runs scaffold() and asserts detectAnchors(tmp).kit is still false and the stub Presentation.tsx is unchanged. The mechanism is in setup.mjs scaffold() (lines 218-237). It selects the FILE_GROUPS for the missing anchors, but then skips every destination file that already exists, even files that belong to an anchor it just classified as missing. It returns normally without an error or warning, so a detected missing anchor stays unscaffolded. SKILL.md section 2 (lines 53-55) tells the agent to rely on this helper and to never overwrite an existing file, and it gives no other path for completing such an anchor. The review guidance says to fail when a delivered helper implements the branch differently. This is a delivered, asserted behavior inside the named partial-scaffold scenario, not a hypothetical input. Judges A and C are right that SKILL.md says to copy only missing anchors, that existing files are skipped, and that package.json is merged. Those points show that present anchors are not disturbed. engineering-tests-isolate-resourcesengineering-presentation-code-and-tests0.375 of 0.375 (minor)passI&#39;m ruling Judge A and Judge B&#39;s pass. Every test that starts a preview or a browser does it through the shared runtime helpers. startPreview gets its port from freePort(), which listens on port 0 and returns the port the OS assigns, then passes that port with --strictPort. No test file hardcodes a preview port, so the two integration files cannot collide. startPreview spawns the Vite server itself (process.execPath running vite.js), not an npm or npx wrapper. Its stop() sends SIGTERM, escalates to SIGKILL after 3 seconds, and resolves only on that process&#39;s &#39;exit&#39; event, so the server itself is terminated and awaited. The two browser tests, recordTransition in inspect.test.ts and the host-route case in partial-scaffold.test.ts, run `await browser.close(); await preview.stop()` in a finally block, so both started processes are terminated whether the assertions pass or fail. The e2e verify tests start no preview themselves; they run verify synchronously and, on the failure paths, assert that the port verify printed is closed afterwards (&#39;preview left running&#39;). Judge C is right that launchBrowser() is awaited before the try block, so a rejected browser launch would skip preview.stop(). That reason does not decide this criterion. Its guidance names two failures: a shared hardcoded port, and killing only an npm or npx wrapper. It does not name browser-launch failure; that scenario belongs to engineering-preview-terminated-on-every-exit, which covers the scripts, not the tests. The tests the candidate actually runs launch the browser and reach the finally cleanup, and the rules say not to fail on a hypothetical failure path the guidance does not name. requirement. 1. **Ports are allocated dynamically.** `freePort()` listens on port 0 and returns the port the OS assigns. `startPreview` takes its port from `freePort()` and passes it with `--strictPort`. Both quoted browser tests get their preview through `startPreview`, so neither uses a fixed port. 2. **Every started process is terminated.** `startPreview` spawns the Vite server directly (`process.execPath` running `vite.js`), not an npm or npx wrapper, so stopping the child stops the server itself. `stop()` sends SIGTERM, escalates to SIGKILL after 3 seconds, and resolves only on the child&#39;s &#39;exit&#39; event. If the server never becomes ready, `startPreview` also calls `stop()` before it throws. `recordTransition` and the host-route test both run `await browser.close(); await preview.stop()` in a finally block, so the browser and the server are cleaned up whether the assertions pass or fail. The e2e verify tests start no preview themselves; on the failure paths they check that the port verify printed is closed afterwards. There is one gap: `launchBrowser()` is awaited before the try block, so a rejected browser launch would skip `preview.stop()`. The guidance for this criterion names only two failures: a shared hardcoded port, and killing only an npm or npx wrapper. A browser launch failure is not one of them, and the audit rules say not to fail on a hypothetical path the guidance does not name. Its stop() sends SIGTERM, escalates to SIGKILL after 3 seconds, and resolves only on that process&#39;s &#39;exit&#39; event, so the server itself is terminated and awaited. Judge C is right that launchBrowser() is awaited before the try block, so a rejected browser launch would skip preview.stop(). That reason does not decide this criterion. Its guidance names two failures: a shared hardcoded port, and killing only an npm or npx wrapper. It does not name browser-launch failure; that scenario belongs to engineering-preview-terminated-on-every-exit, which covers the scripts, not the tests. dispute_checks{"demo-integration":[],"scene-kit":[],"presentation-skill":[{"id":"skill-partial-scaffold","classification":"confirmed","rationale":"The criterion requires that when some but not all anchors are present, the skill scaffolds the missing anchors. After scaffold() runs, the test explicitly asserts detectAnchors(tmp).kit is still false and the stub is unchanged. This is because scaffold() skips every existing destination file, even files belonging to an anchor it has just found missing. It returns normally with no error, so the helper leaves the missing anchors unscaffolded. That fact does not defeat the pass under the rubric contract. The guidance names two failure modes. The first is a transition check that converts an absent or non-numeric hook into a number that still satisfies its comparison. The second is an unreadable step count that makes the verifier step through no steps and still pass. Neither occurs here. Every transition check (i &gt; 0) uses waitForIndex, which compares the raw attribute string to String(i). No numeric conversion takes place, so a missing or non-numeric index can never satisfy it. The step count is validated with !(count &gt; 0): Number(null) gives 0 and Number(&#39;abc&#39;) gives NaN, and both fail with &#39;data-step-count is missing or zero&#39;. Step 0 is the starting state, not a transition, so not checking it does not count as &#39;treating a missing hook as progress&#39;. The guidance&#39;s Number(null) === 0 example describes a comparison fooled by conversion. No such comparison exists here. The auditor&#39;s case, an invalid initial index followed by valid advancing indices, is a hypothetical input the candidate does not produce and the guidance does not name. The required test of a step that fails to render or advance is present. The uncaught-exception test asserts a non-zero exit and &#39;phase: render, step 6&#39;.
